title: PMI Has a Request Date, an Automatic Date—and a Loan-Specific Rulebook
subtitle: For many conventional mortgages, asking to end private mortgage insurance and having it end automatically are different milestones. Here’s how to find the dates that matter on your own loan.

body: The charge that can outlast its purpose

A mortgage payment can contain several different costs, and private mortgage insurance is easy to overlook among them. PMI generally applies to some conventional loans when the down payment was below 20%. It protects the lender—not the borrower—if the loan defaults. That makes it worth understanding what must happen for the charge to end, rather than assuming it disappears when the home has gained value or the loan feels well established. [1]

For many loans covered by federal borrower-paid PMI rules, three milestones matter: the point when a borrower may request cancellation, the point when the servicer generally must terminate PMI automatically, and a midpoint backstop. The first is commonly tied to a loan balance of 80% of the home’s original value; the second to 78%; the third to the midpoint of the loan’s amortization period. Each operates differently, and none is a universal promise for every kind of mortgage insurance. [2]
The 80% point is a request—not an automatic switch

A borrower can generally submit a written request to cancel PMI when the principal balance is scheduled to reach 80% of the home’s original value. The relevant figure is not simply what a current online estimate says the home could sell for. Check the value and cancellation terms recorded for your loan, then ask the servicer how it calculates the threshold and which date it has on file. Extra principal payments may affect when a balance reaches a threshold, but ask how your servicer treats them before relying on a date from a general calculator. [2]

A request also has conditions. The borrower must be current and have a good payment history, certify that there are no junior liens, and provide evidence that the property’s value has not fallen below its original value if the servicer requires it. A request is a process to begin, not a guarantee that the charge will stop that day. Ask what documents are needed, where to send the request, and whether any property or loan-specific conditions apply. [2]

For covered loans, PMI generally must terminate automatically when the principal balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the home’s original value, provided the borrower is current. Unlike the 80% route, this is not ordinarily triggered by the borrower sending a cancellation request. The distinction matters: if a servicer’s records show the loan is approaching 78%, a borrower should still check the account and contact the servicer if PMI remains after the relevant date. [2][3]

“Scheduled” is important. The automatic-termination date is generally based on the original amortization schedule, not on a homeowner’s estimate of present market value or an informal calculation of equity. Making extra payments may change the actual balance sooner without necessarily changing the scheduled date used for automatic termination. If the dates appear inconsistent, ask the servicer to explain its calculation in writing.

If PMI has not ended earlier, federal law provides a further termination rule at the midpoint of the loan’s amortization period, generally when the borrower is current. This backstop can matter when a loan’s balance is not on track to reach 78% by that point. It is not the same as a calendar midpoint in the time a person has owned the home: it refers to the amortization period for the loan. The legal framework also contains exceptions, so the loan documents and servicer’s explanation matter. [3]

These milestones concern covered borrower-paid private mortgage insurance, not every product people call “mortgage insurance.” FHA and VA mortgage insurance have different requirements, and different rules apply when a lender pays for the mortgage insurance. If a statement or closing paperwork uses unfamiliar terms, ask the servicer what type of coverage the loan has and which cancellation rule applies. [2]
When rising home value enters the conversation

A homeowner may ask whether PMI can be removed under lender or servicer standards beyond the baseline legal milestones. CFPB says some lenders and servicers may allow removal under their own standards, and loan investors including Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac often have their own guidelines, which cannot be less favorable to borrowers than the legal requirements. [2]

Ask the servicer to identify the rule it is applying, whether a new valuation is required, who arranges it, and who pays. A recent sale nearby, a tax assessment, or a homeowner’s own estimate may not satisfy the servicer’s requirements. Get the answer and any next steps in writing, and compare them with the mortgage documents rather than treating a general online rule as a decision on your loan.
A practical review for two people

Set aside 15 calm minutes with the mortgage statement, closing or PMI disclosure paperwork, payment history, and access to the servicer’s official contact channel. Start by identifying whether the charge is borrower-paid PMI or another form of mortgage insurance. Then find the original value and the loan’s scheduled 80%, 78%, and midpoint dates if they are disclosed. If they are not, ask the servicer to provide the applicable dates and explain how they were calculated. [2]

Next, check whether payments are current and whether there are other liens or conditions that could affect a request. Write down the servicer’s exact instructions for making a written cancellation request, including the address or secure portal, required documents, and expected review process. One person can ask the questions while the other records the answers, then switch roles and read the next step back. The goal is not to predict approval from a balance alone; it is to leave with the right rule, the relevant date, and a clear route to verify what happens next.
